Q: Access query for finding whether participants in a program returned in the next season A:

Use "self" JOIN.
You can check, whether exists row with next season in "tblProgramSubTable".
JOIN condition is

 ON ( t2.ParticipantId=t1.ParticipantId  -- same Participant
   and t2.ProgramSubId<>t1.ProgramSubId  -- avoid duplicate with same row
   and  (
         -- this year - next season ('Fall' after 'Spring')
      ( (t1.[Year]=t2.[Year]) AND (t1.[Season]='Spring' AND t2.[Season]='Fall') )
         -- or next year first season  ('Spring' after 'Fall' of previous year)
   or ( (t2.[Year] = (t1.[Year]+1)) AND (t1.[Season] ='Fall' AND t2.[Season]='Spring')             
  )
)

SELECT t1.ProgramSubID  , t1.ParticipantID, t1.Year as year1, t1.Season as season1
   ,iif( isnull(t2.ParticipantId) ,'No', 'Yes') as  ReturnNext
FROM tblProgramSubtable as t1 
LEFT JOIN tblProgramSubtable AS t2 
   ON ( t2.ParticipantId=t1.ParticipantId and t2.ProgramSubId<>t1.ProgramSubId
      and  (
           ( (t1.[Year] = t2.[Year]) AND ( t1.[Season] ='Spring' AND  t2.[Season]='Fall') )
        or ( (t2.[Year] = (t1.[Year]+1)) AND ( t1.[Season] ='Fall' AND  t2.[Season]='Spring') )
     )
)
order by t1.ProgramSubId

Or more verbose

SELECT t1.ProgramSubID  , t1.ParticipantID, t1.Year as year1, t1.Season as season1
   ,iif( isnull(t2.ParticipantId) ,'No', 'Yes') as  ReturnNext
  ,iif(t1.Season='Spring','Fall','Spring')+' '+ cstr(iif(t1.Season='Spring',t1.Year,t1.Year+1)) +iif( isnull(t2.ParticipantId) ,' record does not exists ', ' record exists') as Explanation
  ,iif(isnull(
              (select max(Season) as nextSeason from tblProgramSubtable as t3 
               where (    (t3.Year=t1.Year and t1.Season='Spring' and t3.Season='Fall') 
                       or (t3.Year=(t1.Year+1) and t1.Season='Fall' and t3.Season='Spring')  )
              )),' Data not entered','')  as comment
FROM tblProgramSubtable as t1 
LEFT JOIN tblProgramSubtable AS t2 
   ON ( t2.ParticipantId=t1.ParticipantId and t2.ProgramSubId<>t1.ProgramSubId
      and  (
           ( (t1.[Year] = t2.[Year]) AND ( t1.[Season] ='Spring' AND  t2.[Season]='Fall') )
        or ( (t2.[Year] = (t1.[Year]+1)) AND ( t1.[Season] ='Fall' AND  t2.[Season]='Spring') )
     )
)
order by t1.ProgramSubId

Q: Why is the namespace not needed in "friend class" for the base class? A:

In a nutshell, name lookup looks for the InnerClass first in the scope of OtherClass. Next it inspects the base classes. In tn::InnerClass<OtherClass> the injected classname is just InnerClass.

Q: Rails autosave not saving changes to associations A:

Just spent a while fighting this issue. Besides setting autosave properly, it is important to understand what happens on the Database only, and what happens in the collection in memory. Autosave can only handle what is in the collection.

The .last() method gets translated into SQL like ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1, so this happens only on the Database.

To make it happen in memory, we must use ruby semantics, e.g. @child = @parent.childs[-1].

We can check this in the debugger, there are two helpful methods:

  Model.collection.loaded?
  Model.changed_for_autosave?

So let's play:

class ChildController
   def update
     @child = Child.find(params[:id])
     debugger
     ...

     SQL Child Load () SELECT "childs".* FROM "childs"
                        WHERE "childs"."id" = 28 LIMIT 1 
(rdbg) child1 = @child
 id: 28,
 content: "bla bla",

(rdbg) child2 = @child.parent.childs.last
     SQL Child Load () SELECT "childs".* FROM "childs"
                       WHERE "childs"."parent_id" = 9 LIMIT 1
                       ORDER BY "childs"."id" DESC LIMIT 1
 id: 28,
 content: "bla bla",

(rdbg) @child.parent.childs.loaded?
false

Now we have two entities of the same child, but still nothing loaded into the collection. You could save these entities separately in a transaction with multiple .save! operations, but not with autosave.

(rdbg) child1[:content] = "no works"
(rdbg) child1[:content]
"no works"
(rdbg) child2[:content]
"bla bla"
(rdbg) @child.parent.changed_for_autosave?
false

They are independent entities, and not related to the parent.
Now access it in ruby and bring it into memory as a collection:

(rdbg) @child.parent.childs[-1].content = "works"
(rdbg) @child.parent.childs.loaded?
true
(rdbg) @child.parent.changed_for_autosave?
true

Corollary: if you need a specific record (and not just the last one), the .find() and .where() methods on the collection will again only do SQL. To do it in ruby and bring the collection into memory, you can use the .select() method, like so:

child = @child.parent.childs.select do |ch|
  ch.id == params[:id]
end.first

And finally, the reason for all this behaviour might be, if you have really big collections, it is more performant to treat them in the database as much as possible.

Q: Telegram NewMessage Event Handler Not Firing for Large Supergroups (GramJS) A:

Got same problem something around month ago. It's look' like problem with GramJS itself.

And due to poor support for this library, you may not be able to find the solution.

But! I find that there are an another opensource lib that actually work! It is a fork of GramJS with simillar syntax. Check this out on Github: https://github.com/sanyok12345/teleproto

And on NPM: https://www.npmjs.com/package/teleproto
